title: Motion to Compel Production of Non-Public Version of the Filing, Request for Extended Comment Period, and Limited Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. to Dayton Power and Light Company's 09/10/2026 Construction Service Agreement filing under ER26-3752.

documents.name: ER26-3752 Buckeye Comments.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

         The Dayton Power and Light Company                        Docket No. ER26-3752-000


                        MOTION TO COMPEL PRODUCTION OF
                        NON-PUBLIC VERSION OF THE FILING,
               REQUEST FOR EXTENDED COMMENT PERIOD, AND LIMITED
                       COMMENTS OF BUCKEYE POWER, INC.

           Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

September 11, 2026 Combined Notice of Filings #1, 1 Buckeye Power, Inc. (“Buckeye”) 2

respectfully submits these limited comments on the September 10, 2026 filing 3 by the

Dayton Power and Light Company (“AES Ohio”) in the above-captioned proceeding.

The filing contains a Construction Service Agreement (“CSA”), with a form electric

service agreement (“ESA”) attached as Exhibit E, between AES Ohio and an unidentified

data center customer.

           As an initial matter, AES Ohio has not provided Buckeye a copy of the

unredacted CSA, despite Buckeye representatives having signed the protective agreement

included in AES Ohio’s filing and the requirements of 18 C.F.R. § 388.112. The

Commission should order AES Ohio to provide the unredacted CSA to those that have

signed the protective agreement and reopen the comment period to allow comments

based on review of the complete filing. Unless and until AES Ohio has provided

interested parties an opportunity to review its filing in full, the Commission should not

accept the filing.

        Notwithstanding any issues with this particular CSA that review of the full

agreement may reveal, Buckeye generally supports the steps AES Ohio is taking in this

proceeding to protect all transmission customers of AES Ohio from potential stranded

transmission costs, as Buckeye has stated in previous filings on other AES Ohio

Construction Service Agreements for data center loads, 4. In its Show Cause Order to PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) relating to large load interconnections, the Commission

recognized the importance of a “mechanism to help ensure that Eligible Customers taking

transmission service on behalf of large loads (as opposed to other transmission

customers) bear the risk of, and are ultimately responsible for, the costs incurred to

provide them with the requested transmission service, including the costs of any needed

Network Upgrades.” 5

        As an interim measure, Buckeye supports AES Ohio’s continued approach of

filing CSAs with the Commission along with an express commitment to apply protections

in its retail data center agreements through its formula rate in Attachment H-15 of the

PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff. This approach, if properly effectuated in future

filings, should protect all wholesale transmission customers, and their retail customers,

from transmission cost shifting caused by large loads. But, as the investment in new and

Light Co., Docket No. ER26-1463 (Mar. 13, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260313-5222; Comments of Buckeye

5077; Motion for Leave to File Comments Out-of-Time and Limited Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc.,
Dayton Power & Light Co., Docket No. ER25-192 (Nov. 21, 2024), eLibrary No. 20241121-5196.
5
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211, P 80 (“Show Cause Order”), errata 196 FERC ¶ 1,122,
reh’g denied 196 FERC ¶ 61,214 (2026).
                                                   -3-

upgraded transmission to serve new data center loads further balloons, it is increasingly

urgent that cost treatment details be clearly and explicitly addressed. Buckeye expects

that, as a result of the Show Cause Order, AES Ohio and other PJM transmission owners

will propose a consistent, clear process through a pro forma agreement to protect all

wholesale transmission customers (particularly those not serving the data center load

triggering the upgrades) from potential transmission cost shifting caused by the large

load. 6 Buckeye reserves all rights with respect to such future filings, including, but not

limited to, filings in response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order.

           I.       MOTION TO COMPEL

           “In accordance with 18 C.F.R. § 388.122(b)(2)(i),” AES Ohio filed a proposed

form of protective agreement (based on the Commission’s Model Protective Order)

because it filed both a privileged version of the CSA and a public version that redacts

information AES Ohio states is confidential. 7 After moving to intervene in this

proceeding, Buckeye emailed AES Ohio, including the contact listed in AES Ohio’s

filing, copies of the non-disclosure agreement’s signature page executed by several

Buckeye representatives on September 22, 2026. 8 Under the Commission’s rules, “[i]f

no objection to disclosure is filed, the filer must provide a copy of the complete, non-



6
  The Commission granted motions for abeyance to make the compliance deadline for the Show Cause
Order November 16, 2026. In its order granting those motions, the Commission explained that the
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners “anticipate that their FPA section 205 filing(s) will include: (1) pro
forma cost recovery agreements and rates for new transmission services for flexible large loads and
electrically proximate large loads or co-located loads; and (2) any financial penalties applied to customers
that fail to meet their contractual service limits with respect to any new transmission services.” PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,129, P 5 (2026).
7
    AES Ohio Filing, Transmittal Letter at 10.
8
  See 18 C.F.R. § 388.112(B)(2)(iii) (“Any person who . . . has filed a motion to intervene or notice of
intervention in the proceeding may make a written request to the filer for a copy of the complete, non-
public version of the document.”).
                                                  -4-

public document to the requesting person within 5 days after receipt of the written

request that is accompanied by an executed copy of the protective agreement.” 9 AES

Ohio did not file any objection to providing Buckeye with the unredacted CSA, nor did

it otherwise inform Buckeye of any objection. Buckeye followed up on its original

September 22, 2026, request on September 24, 2026, and was told that AES Ohio’s

legal representative will address this matter. Buckeye did not receive any follow-up

from AES Ohio after that exchange, nor after Buckeye attempted to call on September

29, 2026. To date, AES Ohio has not provided the non-public version of the CSA to

Buckeye nor explained why it has not done so.

           Without access to the full agreement, Buckeye cannot evaluate whether AES

Ohio has satisfied its burden of showing that the agreement is just, reasonable, and not

unduly discriminatory. Review of the full CSA is essential to understanding whether, as

AES Ohio claims, it protects other customers from the costs caused by this data center

customer, and whether such protections are adequate in light of the anticipate costs.

Indeed, the Commission has specifically recognized the importance of transparency in

the context of new large loads. 10

           Allowing AES Ohio’s inaction (whether intentional or not) to deny interested

parties that executed the protective agreement access to the full CSA—particularly

without any explanation—would set a dangerous precedent that encourages secrecy

around new large load developments. There is no reason that the full CSA cannot be



9
    Id. § 388.112(B)(2)(iv).
10
  Show Cause Order P 74 (“We are concerned that without sufficient transparency regarding the Network
Upgrades, and their associated costs, needed to provide transmission service to Eligible Customers on
behalf of large loads, stakeholders may lack information and visibility regarding the costs driven by large

                                                  -5-

share with interested parties, subject to protections for confidential information based on

the Commission’s well-established Model Protective Order. The Commission should

therefore direct AES Ohio to provide the non-public CSA to Buckeye, and any other

participants that signed the protective agreement, and establish a new comment window.

The Commission should not accept AES Ohio’s filing unless and until interested parties

have had an opportunity to review and comment on the full filing.

           II.      COMMENTS

                  A.     Buckeye supports AES Ohio’s wholesale solution to protect all
                         wholesale transmission customers from transmission cost-shifting.

           Buckeye supports AES Ohio’s proactive acknowledgement to the Commission

of the potential impact that the new data center at issue in this proceeding could have

other customers that pay Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates. Buckeye

understands almost $600 million in transmission investment is expected, not including

any required regional transmission upgrades. 11 If the data center load does not show up,

or is not sustained, as expected, these significant costs could be shifted to other

customers as a result of AES Ohio’s intent “to seek rolled-in rate treatment for those

costs.” 12

           Buckeye appreciates AES Ohio’s stated intention to protect other customers

“from having to shoulder the costs of those facilities in the event the Data Center does

8 (May 8, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-
groups/committees/teac/2026/20260508/20260508-item-05---dayton-supplemental-projects.pdf
(presenting, at the May 8, 2026 Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee meeting, a $591 million
supplemental project in the vicinity of the Eldean Substation in Piqua, Ohio).
12
     AES Ohio Filing, Transmittal Letter at 4.
                                               -6-

not achieve commercial operations or take a minimum level of service.” 13 AES Ohio

explains that the CSA should ensure that the data center will “take a minimum level of

transmission service that will produce revenues that equal or exceed the costs of the

Network Upgrades necessary . . . thereby protecting AES Ohio and its other

transmission customers from potential adverse cost shifts associated with rolled in

pricing for the new service.” 14

            Importantly, AES Ohio acknowledges that its CSA with the data center

customer will not, on its own, protect customers paying Commission-jurisdictional

transmission rates. Instead, specific action before this Commission is needed: 15

                    In order to avoid the potential for double recovery of
                    Network Upgrade costs, AES Ohio agrees that, if the
                    Network Upgrade costs are rolled into its transmission rates
                    under Attachment H-15 of the PJM OATT and if Customer
                    subsequently makes a payment to AES Ohio of the Network
                    Upgrade costs incurred under CSA Section 7 and 14 or
                    Exhibit E – ESA Section 2.c.ii of the CSA . . . AES Ohio will
                    appropriately reflect Customer’s payment in its
                    transmission cost of service under Attachment H-15.
                    However, rate treatment of such proceeds should be
                    appropriately addressed in a future AES Ohio rate case, not
                    this proceeding.

            Thus, AES Ohio recognizes that the data center’s payments to AES Ohio, in the

event that it does not achieve or sustain a minimum level of service for an extended

time, must be appropriately reflected in the transmission rates on file with the

Commission. Otherwise, the goal of protecting other customers from data center-caused

costs will not be achieved, contrary to the Commission’s obligations under the Federal



13
     Id. at 1.
14
     Id. at 8-9.
15
     Id. at 9 n.19 (emphasis added).
                                                       -7-

Power Act (“FPA”) to ensure just, reasonable, and not discriminatory rates. 16

                  B.     Critical cost treatment details will need to be addressed in future
                         filings, and Buckeye reserves all rights with respect to such future
                         filings.

           AES Ohio indicates that the rate treatment of payments from the data center in

the event that it triggers the protective provisions of the CSA will be “addressed in a

future AES Ohio rate case” filed with the Commission, 17 and the Commission has

previously held that its acceptance of a CSA “does not impact or pre-judge any future

determination regarding the treatment of Network Upgrade costs” of the facilities

contemplated under that CSA.” 18 Consistent with those prior orders, Commission

acceptance of the CSA in this proceeding should not prejudge the outcome of any

future filings, including but not limited to the critical filings committed to in AES

Ohio’s filing. Buckeye reserves all rights with respect to any such future proceeding(s).

           Although this approach of deferring rate treatment details may be appropriate

for this proceeding, it underscores the urgent need for greater clarity and certainty

about the cost treatment of data center-driven transmission costs. Buckeye appreciates

AES Ohio’s and the Commission’s intent to protect other wholesale transmission

customers, but today customers remain in the dark as to how such protections will be

implemented. AES Ohio does not provide any details on the substance of such future

filings, such as how data center payments pursuant to the CSA’s protective provisions

would be input into AES Ohio’s Attachment H-15 or any revisions to the Attachment




16
     16 U.S.C. § 824d.
17
     AES Ohio Filing, Transmittal Letter at 9 n.19.
18
   See, e.g., Dayton Power & Light Co., 195 FERC ¶ 61,239, P 15 (2026); Dayton Power & Light Co., 192
FERC ¶ 61,103, P 13 (2025) (same); Dayton Power & Light Co., 189 FERC ¶ 61,220, P 23 (2024) (same).
                                                    -8-

H-15 formula needed to properly reflect such payments in rates. Given the billions of

dollars being invested in new and upgraded transmission, it is critical to provide all

stakeholders certainty on how exactly costs will be allocated.

           These rate treatment details will be critical to ensuring that the data center’s

payments to AES Ohio result in protection of all wholesale transmission customers—

not just AES Ohio itself, consistent with the Commission’s Show Cause Order 19 and

Commission’s orders accepting AES Ohio’s prior CSA filings.20 Indeed, the

Commission’s Show Cause Order “preliminarily find[s] that it appears reasonable for

filers of formula rates to provide a separate workpaper in the annual informational

filing describing how any payments made pursuant to a cost recovery agreement are

reflected in the transmission owner’s transmission formula rate.” 21

           In the filings in response to the Show Cause Order, Buckeye expects

transmission owners, such as AES Ohio, to explain the precise manner in which data

center payments made under agreements, such as the CSA, will be reflected in their

transmission formula rates. Absent a demonstration that those costs are properly

reflected in rates, the significant transmission investments caused by new data center

loads could result in unreasonable cost increases for other wholesale transmission

customers.

       III.     CONCLUSION

              For the reasons stated above, the Commission should take these comments

into consideration. The Commission should direct AES Ohio to provide the non-public

CSA to Buckeye, and any others that signed the protective agreement, and establish a

new comment period.
